Renal and Genitourinary Disorders

Acute Urinary Retention

Acute urinary retention is painful inability to void despite bladder filling. The ED job is decompression without urethral injury, identification of dangerous causes, and clear disposition.

Board trap: Do not force repeated blind catheter attempts. Pain, resistance, trauma history, or postsurgical urethra/prostate history should trigger safer technique or urology.

Acute Urinary Retention

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

AUR is common, especially in older men with benign prostatic hyperplasia. Women have AUR far less often, so retention in women deserves a broader search for gynecologic, neurologic, postoperative, pharmacologic, or obstructive causes.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Retention occurs when outlet obstruction, detrusor failure, impaired coordination, medications, pain, inflammation, clots, neurologic disease, or postoperative physiology prevent voiding. Prolonged obstruction can cause AKI and postobstructive diuresis after relief.

CLINICAL FEATURES

The classic presentation is suprapubic pain, distention, urgency, and inability to void. Older patients may report overflow, abdominal discomfort, agitation, or nonspecific symptoms. History must cover prostate symptoms, medications, urinary instrumentation, urethral trauma, neurologic deficits, infection symptoms, hematuria, stones, cancer, and recent surgery/anesthesia.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Rosen emphasizes bedside diagnostic patterns by physical exam; Tintinalli supplies the Ch92 procedural flow, management steps, and every Ch92 table/figure.

DIAGNOSIS

Diagnosis is clinical and confirmed by bladder scan or bedside ultrasound when uncertain. UA helps identify UTI or hematuria; renal function and electrolytes are considered with prolonged obstruction, bilateral obstruction risk, renal disease, or ill appearance. PSA is not an ED diagnostic test for acute retention.

TREATMENT

The central treatment is bladder decompression. A standard 14F to 18F Foley usually works, but difficulty may come from BPH, meatal stenosis, stricture, urethral injury, or postsurgical anatomy. Urology is needed early for suspected urethral trauma, complex reconstruction, radical prostatectomy, acute febrile prostatitis, or failed safe attempts.

Tintinalli source

Table 92-4

Steps in ED evaluation and management of acute urinary retention.

URETHRAL CATHETERIZATION TECHNIQUE

Use lubrication and adequate insertion depth. In uncircumcised males, reduce the foreskin after placement. Do not inflate the balloon until urine flows and the catheter is advanced into the bladder; severe pain during inflation suggests balloon inflation in the urethra. If a standard Foley fails, try a coude catheter with the tip anterior/cephalad; do not keep forcing against resistance.

SUPRAPUBIC CATHETERIZATION TECHNIQUE

Suprapubic catheterization is for failed urethral catheterization when bladder decompression is needed and pelvic trauma/abnormal anatomy is not suspected. Ultrasound must show a distended bladder and no bowel in the path. Obturator and Seldinger techniques both require controlled entry and confirmation of urine flow before balloon inflation.

POSTCATHETERIZATION CARE

Reassess pain relief, urine output, hematuria, vitals, and renal/electrolyte risk. Large ongoing output may signal postobstructive diuresis; patients with azotemia, dehydration, electrolyte derangement, or very high urine output may need admission and replacement fluids. Asymptomatic bacteriuria after catheterization does not require antibiotics.

DISPOSITION AND FOLLOW-UP

Most uncomplicated AUR patients go home with Foley/leg bag, catheter care instructions, return precautions, alpha blocker if appropriate, and urology follow-up. Admit sepsis, AKI/electrolyte disturbance, neurologic compression, serious underlying illness, unresolved hematuria/clot retention, urinary tract injury, or inability to manage the catheter.

SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS

URINE LEAKAGE AROUND A SUPRAPUBIC CATHETER

Leakage may reflect detrusor spasm, constipation, infection, obstruction, or catheter encrustation. Evaluate drainage, infection, and catheter function; urology manages chronic catheter problems.

FEMALES WITH URINARY RETENTION

Female retention is uncommon and should prompt pelvic exam and assessment for pelvic mass/prolapse, pregnancy-related causes, neurologic disease, medications, infection, and postoperative factors. Alpha blockers are not reliably helpful in women.

GROSS HEMATURIA AND CLOT RETENTION

Gross hematuria can create painful clot retention and sympathetic vital sign changes. Treat with 20F to 24F triple-lumen catheter, manual clot irrigation, continuous bladder irrigation, and urology when clots or bleeding persist. Persistent gross hematuria is not a simple Foley-discharge problem.

POSTOPERATIVE URINARY RETENTION

Postoperative retention follows anesthesia, pain, immobility, opioids, and anticholinergic exposure. Decompress, address triggers, and arrange trial of voiding or follow-up according to surgical context.

POSTPARTUM URINARY RETENTION

Postpartum retention is associated with prolonged labor, epidural anesthesia, instrumental delivery, perineal trauma, edema, and pain. Bladder decompression prevents overdistention injury while obstetric follow-up addresses recurrence.
